extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and critics of English poetry (readers of The Spectator interested in Milton's Paradise Lost)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing Book IV of Milton's Paradise Lost, focusing on which aspects to look for (descriptive still-life, dramatic machines/speeches, and the conduct of principal characters) and how diction and invention should be applied. Also prescribes a short practical exercise in self-examination (keeping a journal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a one-week journal for self-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: I would, however, recommend to every one of my Readers, the keeping a Journal of their Lives for one Week, and setting down punctually their whole Series of Employments during that Space of Time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice 'would give them a true State of themselves, and incline them to consider seriously what they are about.' One Day would rectify the Omissions of another, and make a Man weigh all those indifferent Actions, which, though they are easily forgotten, must certainly be accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the nature of the part one plays in life
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Men, while they are in Health, consider well the Nature of the Part they are engaged in, and what Figure it will make in the Minds of those they leave behind them: Whether it was worth coming into the World for; whether it be suitable to a reasonable Being; in short, whether it appears Graceful in this Life, or will turn to an Advantage in the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the image of an actor 'going off the Stage with your Applause' (Augustus) to judge whether one's life and actions will be remembered or praised; reflect on whether ordinary habits (eating, drinking, sleeping, buffoonery, sycophancy) will be seen as praiseworthy after death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse an epic's beauties under three heads
rubrics_metrics.description: We may consider the Beauties of the Fourth Book under three Heads. In the first are those Pictures of Still-Life ... In the next are the Machines, which comprehend the Speeches and Behaviour of the good and bad Angels. In the last is the Conduct of Adam and Eve, who are the Principal Actors in the Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticising an epic (here: Paradise Lost, Book IV), explicitly separate and attend to (1) descriptive still-life/pictures (scenery, objects), (2) dramatic machinery (speeches, actions of supernatural agents), and (3) the moral and dramatic conduct of principal human characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lavish ornamented diction on weak/unactive parts (descriptive still-life)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Description of Paradise, the Poet has observed Aristotle's Rule of lavishing all the Ornaments of Diction on the weak unactive Parts of the Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive passages (gardens, rivers, rainbows, the seat of happiness) may properly employ more florid and elaborate expression than active parts. Although excessive descriptive length is ordinarily censurable in heroic poetry, such particularity is 'requisite' here because Paradise is the scene of the principal action and must convey an idea of that happiness from which the first parents fell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure speeches and machines reflect place and internal conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Satan ... being within Prospect of Eden ... is filled with Sentiments different from those which he discovered whilst he was in Hell. The Place inspires him with Thoughts more adapted to it: He reflects upon the happy Condition from which he fell, and breaks forth into a Speech that is softened with several transient Touches of Remorse and Self-accusation: But at length he confirms himself in Impenitence, and in his Design of drawing Man into his own State of Guilt and Misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good dramatic machinery makes characters' speeches and behaviour arise naturally from their situation; it should exhibit conflict of passions (e.g., remorse then hardening to impenitence). Use surprising circumstances and transformations (Satan bounding over walls, perching as a cormorant, hiding as a toad) to give agreeable surprise and to connect the series of adventures; literal description often conceals a moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make principal characters' language and thought consistent with their habitation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is scarce a Speech of Adam or Eve in the whole Poem, wherein the Sentiments and Allusions are not taken from this their delightful Habitation ... their Thoughts are always Paradisiacal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing character dialogue in an epic, ensure the speakers' sentiments and allusions are influenced by their environment (e.g., Adam and Eve's language is coloured by Paradise). As with pastoral or shepherd-actors, the characters' thoughts and diction should retain the tint of their setting throughout their actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's liberty: do not be strictly bound by any single critical rule
rubrics_metrics.description: As the greatest Masters of Critical Learning differ among one another, as to some particular Points in an Epic Poem, I have not bound my self scrupulously to the Rules which any one of them has laid down upon that Art, but have taken the Liberty sometimes to join with one, and sometimes with another, and sometimes to differ from all of them, when I have thought that the Reason of the thing was on my side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a flexible critical method: acknowledge established rules (Aristotle, earlier critics) but feel free to adapt, combine, or depart from them where reason and the particulars of the work justify doing so.
